verses.text: At the end of two full years, Pharaoh dreamed: and behold, he stood by the river.
Behold, there came up out of the river seven cattle, sleek and fat, and they fed in the marsh grass.
Behold, seven other cattle came up after them out of the river, ugly and thin, and stood by the other cattle on the brink of the river.
The ugly and thin cattle ate up the seven sleek and fat cattle. So Pharaoh awoke.
He slept and dreamed a second time: and behold, seven heads of grain came up on one stalk, healthy and good.
Behold, seven heads of grain, thin and blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven healthy and full ears. Pharaoh awoke, and behold, it was a dream.
In the morning, his spirit was troubled, and he sent and called for all of Egypt’s magicians and wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was no one who could interpret them to Pharaoh.
Then the chief cup bearer spoke to Pharaoh, saying, “I remember my faults today.
Pharaoh was angry with his servants, and put me in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, me and the chief baker.
We dreamed a dream in one night, I and he. We dreamed each man according to the interpretation of his dream.
There was with us there a young man, a Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard, and we told him, and he interpreted to us our dreams. To each man according to his dream he interpreted.
As he interpreted to us, so it was. He restored me to my office, and he hanged him.”
Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon. He shaved himself, changed his clothing, and came in to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you, that when you hear a dream you can interpret it.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, “It isn’t in me. God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”
Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, “In my dream, behold, I stood on the brink of the river:
and behold, there came up out of the river seven cattle, fat and sleek. They fed in the marsh grass,
and behold, seven other cattle came up after them, poor and very ugly and thin, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for ugliness.
The thin and ugly cattle ate up the first seven fat cattle,
and when they had eaten them up, it couldn’t be known that they had eaten them, but they were still ugly, as at the beginning. So I awoke.
I saw in my dream, and behold, seven heads of grain came up on one stalk, full and good:
and behold, seven heads of grain, withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them.
The thin heads of grain swallowed up the seven good heads of grain. I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could explain it to me.”
Joseph said to Pharaoh, “The dream of Pharaoh is one. What God is about to do he has declared to Pharaoh.
The seven good cattle are seven years; and the seven good heads of grain are seven years. The dream is one.
The seven thin and ugly cattle that came up after them are seven years, and also the seven empty heads of grain blasted with the east wind; they will be seven years of famine.
That is the thing which I spoke to Pharaoh. What God is about to do he has shown to Pharaoh.
Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt.
There will arise after them seven years of famine, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will consume the land,
and the plenty will not be known in the land by reason of that famine which follows; for it will be very grievous.
The dream was doubled to Pharaoh, because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.
“Now therefore let Pharaoh look for a discreet and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint overseers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt’s produce in the seven plenteous years.
Let them gather all the food of these good years that come, and lay up grain under the hand of Pharaoh for food in the cities, and let them keep it.
The food will be for a store to the land against the seven years of famine, which will be in the land of Egypt; that the land not perish through the famine.”
The thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants.
Pharaoh said to his servants, “Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Because God has shown you all of this, there is no one so discreet and wise as you.
You shall be over my house, and according to your word will all my people be ruled. Only in the throne I will be greater than you.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Behold, I have set you over all the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh took off his signet ring from his hand, and put it on Joseph’s hand, and arrayed him in robes of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck,
and he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had. They cried before him, “Bow the knee!” He set him over all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I am Pharaoh, and without you shall no man lift up his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphenath-Paneah; and he gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On as a wife. Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt.
In the seven plenteous years the earth produced abundantly.
He gathered up all the food of the seven years which were in the land of Egypt, and laid up the food in the cities: the food of the field, which was around every city, he laid up in the same.
Joseph laid up grain as the sand of the sea, very much, until he stopped counting, for it was without number.
To Joseph were born two sons before the year of famine came, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore to him.
Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh,  “For”, he said, “God has made me forget all my toil, and all my father’s house.”
The name of the second, he called Ephraim : “For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
The seven years of plenty, that were in the land of Egypt, came to an end.
The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.”
The famine was over all the surface of the earth. Joseph opened all the store houses, and sold to the Egyptians. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt.
All countries came into Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain, because the famine was severe in all the earth.

footnotes.content: Two years pass—a long silence. But God had not forgotten. Pharaoh himself becomes the vessel through which the Lord speaks, though he knows it not yet. When the Lord's time arrives, nothing keeps Him waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven sleek cattle rising from the river's abundance—a picture of blessing overflowing, plenty so obvious and full that anyone can see it. Yet even abundance will be tested, and what looks permanent often isn't.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The seven ugly cattle come after, shadowing the joy. In dreams the Lord shows us what we're slow to see awake: blessing and hardship are woven close together, and one may hide itself in the other.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thin devoured the fat. Famine has a way of swallowing up every store we laid up yesterday. Pharaoh wakes shaken—and that shaking is merciful, drawing him to seek what he cannot find in his own wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One dream would have troubled him. Two means the Lord was speaking. A second witness makes the message urgent—the Spirit often repeats what we need most urgently to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The east wind blights grain—a real hardship known to Egypt. The dream speaks in the language of loss Pharaoh knows. The Lord often speaks to us in images drawn from our own world, making the vision unmistakable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thin heads swallowed the full—a strange dream, impossible by nature, yet unforgettable. When God sends a dream, He doesn't whisper; He shakes us awake with something we cannot forget or explain away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Egypt's magicians and wise men stood silent. The best of human learning had nothing to offer. Sometimes the Lord shuts every door but one—so that we will finally turn toward the place where true wisdom dwells.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cupbearer speaks. He had forgotten Joseph's kindness until this moment of need. So often we remember help only when we're desperate—yet the Lord welcomes every sincere cry, even when gratitude comes late.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He confesses his own fault—a good man admitting he carries guilt, remembering that moment of accusation. Honesty opens the door. In our confession the Lord often finds the very opening He was waiting for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One night, two dreamers. Each man had his own vision, yet both pointed toward the same interpreter. When the Lord has something to teach us, He often sends it in multiple voices, each reaching us differently.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A young Hebrew servant—the lowliest mention, a foreigner without rank. Yet he carried the Spirit, and in that moment he was the only one who mattered. The Lord often speaks through those the world has no use for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What he said came to pass. His word proved true—one was restored, one was hanged. When the Lord speaks through a vessel, His word does not return empty. It accomplishes what He purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hastily brought from the dungeon, Joseph shaves and changes. A small detail that shows dignity—he prepares himself to stand before power. The Lord often works through these small acts of readiness and respect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh speaks without knowing this man. He has only heard a rumor of Joseph's gift. Sometimes the Lord opens doors through nothing but a whispered reputation—a faint echo of faithfulness reaches exactly where it needs to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's first word before the throne denies his own wisdom and gives glory to God. This is a real echo—when a believer stands in high places, their first confession still matters most. It shapes everything that follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh speaks his own dream aloud to Joseph. The telling itself becomes a gift—sometimes we understand our own burdens better when we voice them to someone we trust to listen with wisdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The abundance repeated—seven fat cattle fed well. Joseph listens to every detail. In interpretation, as in faith, the particulars matter; generalities miss the truth the Spirit is trying to convey.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ugly and thin—words Pharaoh repeats with force, painting the picture of such extreme poverty and despair as he'd never seen. The Lord shows extremes so we cannot miss them or minimize their weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The eating repeats. Pharaoh's mind returns to the most disturbing image—something unnatural, something that troubles the spirit. The things that haunt us often point to what we most need to prepare for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After eating, no one could tell—a detail that deepens the strangeness and the dread. Scarcity isn't kind; it devours and leaves no trace of what was. Joseph listens to these dark particulars with patience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The grain dream mirrors the cattle—not a new thought but a confirming one. The Lord speaks in echoes. When we hear the same truth in different forms, we're meant to act; the repetition is His hand saying 'Listen.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Withered and blasted grain, thin and empty. Every image speaks of loss and waste—the same terror, the same message, told twice over. Sometimes the Lord must repeat Himself because we're slow to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's magicians couldn't explain it. He stands alone with his fear and his desperation, speaking to a stranger. Sometimes we must come to the end of ourselves before we're ready to truly listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph says 'The dream of Pharaoh is one'—one message, not two different troubles. Then he dares to name the Author: 'What God is about to do.' The boy from the pit speaks as a prophet, and Pharaoh listens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven years is seven years—the dream speaks plainly for those with ears. Joseph doesn't hide behind mystery; he interprets clearly. The gift of understanding is also the gift of speaking truth plainly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven years of famine named. Joseph speaks what no Egyptian magician would dare—hardship is coming, hunger will grip the land. Truth is not always welcome, but the wise know it is far kinder than a comfortable lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again Joseph names God: 'God has shown'—the fourth time in four verses he centers the word in God, not himself. His humility before power is striking. In the presence of Pharaoh, a man of faith stays anchored to his Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven years of great plenty—the coming abundance is real, not a false hope. The Lord both warns of hardship and promises resource. We're called to trust Him in both the fullness and the emptiness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plenty will be forgotten. What seems permanent becomes invisible in the face of hunger. Joseph prepares the hearer to understand: yesterday's abundance means nothing if today we have not prepared for tomorrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Grievous'—Joseph doesn't soften the word. The famine will be severe, pressing, nearly unbearable. A man of God speaks hard truth with clarity, not to terrify but to move the hearer toward wise action.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The dream was doubled because the thing is established by God—the repetition itself is proof of certainty. When the Lord confirms His word twice, there is no room for debate or delay. The time to act is now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph moves from warning to counsel—a discreet and wise man must lead. He does not shrink from giving Pharaoh direction. The faithful aren't afraid to speak what needs speaking, even to the mightiest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Overseers. The fifth part. The plan is practical, specific, measured. Joseph knows that godly wisdom always includes a plan, not merely a warning. Vision without structure is only a dream.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gather the food in the cities. Keep it for the appointed time. Joseph builds a system that will serve all Egypt, not just the powerful. The Lord's wisdom looks toward the survival of the whole people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That the land not perish through famine—the purpose is clear and noble. Everything Joseph proposes flows from one aim: preservation of life, both the land and the people. Wise counsel always serves life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The thing was good in Pharaoh's eyes and in the eyes of all his servants. When wisdom speaks plainly and with purpose, even the powerful recognize it and are moved to receive it. Truth has a weight that flattery never carries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom is the Spirit of God? Pharaoh speaks the deepest truth—he sees what he cannot name in his own language, and he recognizes it. The Spirit's presence is visible to those willing to see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is no one so discreet and wise as you. Pharaoh sees and acknowledges Joseph's gift. A moment ago Joseph was in chains; now the highest power in the land confesses his excellence. The Lord's timing is perfect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You shall be over my house—all the land will be ruled according to Joseph's word. With one sentence, a slave becomes vizier. The Lord raises the humble and does it suddenly, with a finality that shakes kingdoms.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh confirms it again—'I have set you over all the land.' The repetition seals what will soon become evident to all Egypt. When the Lord lifts a man up, He does it openly and with fullness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The signet ring, fine linen, gold chain—the symbols of authority in Egypt were real. Joseph receives not only rank but the outward marks that all Egypt will recognize. The Lord gives both the position and the credentials.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They cried before him, 'Bow the knee!'—the stranger is now the master. Egypt honors Joseph as though he were Egyptian, or higher. The Lord's exaltation leaves no room for doubt; all people acknowledge whom He has raised.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I am Pharaoh, and without you shall no man lift up hand or foot. Pharaoh reserves himself the throne but gives Joseph everything else—absolute authority under the king. It is a generous limit, and Joseph receives it with grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zaphenath-Paneah—Joseph's Egyptian name, a sign that he is woven into the land's life. Asenath, daughter of Potiphera priest of On—he marries into Egypt's priestly class. The Lord places Joseph not as an outsider but as one fully belonging.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh. A real age, a real moment. Joseph was seventeen when Potiphar's house bought him, and now at thirty he is prime minister. The years in between were real, and so is this vindication.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the seven plenteous years the earth produced abundantly. The dreamed abundance arrived—God's word through Joseph came to pass. What He shows always comes; what He purposes He performs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph gathered up all the food and laid it up in the cities. Work began immediately—no delay, no second-guessing. A man who has heard from the Lord acts without hesitation, trusting that the plan is wise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Grain as the sand of the sea, very much, until he stopped counting. The abundance was so great it became uncountable. When the Lord provides, He provides with such fullness that we stop measuring and simply trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before the famine came, Joseph's sons were born. Life continues. Even in a time of faithful work and careful preparation, the Lord gives blessing—family, children, the continuation of love and hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Manasseh—'God has made me forget all my toil and all my father's house.' Joseph's own word about his son reveals his heart: he has been healed. The hurts that seemed permanent have been washed away by the Lord's grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephraim—'God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.' In the place where he suffered, he became fruitful. This is the gospel in a name: the Lord transforms the very ground of our sorrow into soil where blessing grows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The seven years of plenty came to an end. Blessing is not forever in this world; it gives way. Yet Joseph had prepared. The godly don't cling to the good times; they use them to prepare for what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The seven years of famine began. Joseph's word proved true—not as curse but as spoken reality. In all lands there was hunger, yet in Egypt there was bread. Obedience to God's revealed word becomes deliverance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When all the land was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread. Hunger breaks people—they cry out, they look for help. But Pharaoh says, 'Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.' Wisdom in high places knows where to point the desperate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph opened all the store houses and sold to the Egyptians. The bread that was stored comes forth. In the time of need, Joseph becomes the means of life. Preparation in plenty is never wasted if we offer it in faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All countries came into Egypt to buy grain. Joseph's faithfulness rippled outward—not just Egypt survived, but the surrounding lands. One man's obedience to God's word became a bridge of mercy for nations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
